claim: Class A G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) normally function as monomers.
source: Class A G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) normally function as monomers, although evidence from heterologous expression systems suggests that they may sometimes form homodimers and/or heterodimers.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract without specific supporting data in the manuscript.

claim: Evidence from heterologous expression systems suggests that Class A GPCRs may sometimes form homodimers and/or heterodimers.
source: Class A G-protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) normally function as monomers, although evidence from heterologous expression systems suggests that they may sometimes form homodimers and/or heterodimers.
evidence: This is stated as a general finding from prior research, presented as background knowledge.

claim: MORs and DORs co-expressed in transfected cells have been reported to form heterodimers.
source: Previously, MORs and DORs co-expressed in transfected cells have been reported to form heterodimers, and their possible co-localization in neurons has been studied in knock-in mice expressing genetically engineered receptors fused to fluorescent proteins.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from previous studies, referencing prior research.

claim: Single cholinergic neurons in the mouse striatum endogenously express both MORs and DORs.
source: Here, we find that single cholinergic neurons in the mouse striatum endogenously express both MORs and DORs.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data from labeling and electrophysiology.

claim: Receptors on neurons from live brain slices were fluorescently labeled with NAI-A594.
source: The receptors on neurons from live brain slices were fluorescently labeled with a ligand-directed labeling reagent, NAI-A594.
evidence: This describes the experimental method used in the study.

claim: DAMGO (µ-agonist) inhibited spontaneous firing in all cells examined.
source: The selective activation of MORs and DORs, with DAMGO (µ-agonist) and deltorphin (δ-agonist) inhibited spontaneous firing in all cells examined.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Deltorphin (δ-agonist) inhibited spontaneous firing in all cells examined.
source: The selective activation of MORs and DORs, with DAMGO (µ-agonist) and deltorphin (δ-agonist) inhibited spontaneous firing in all cells examined.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: In the continued presence of deltorphin, the firing rate returned to baseline as the result of receptor desensitization.
source: In the continued presence of agonist, the firing rate returned to baseline as the result of receptor desensitization with the application of deltorphin but was less observed with the application of DAMGO.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings showing desensitization.

claim: Desensitization was less observed with the application of DAMGO compared to deltorphin.
source: In the continued presence of agonist, the firing rate returned to baseline as the result of receptor desensitization with the application of deltorphin but was less observed with the application of DAMGO.
evidence: This is a comparative experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: Agonist-induced internalization of DORs was detected.
source: In addition, agonist-induced internalization of DORs but not MORs was detected.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from live-cell imaging experiments.

claim: Agonist-induced internalization of MORs was not detected.
source: In addition, agonist-induced internalization of DORs but not MORs was detected.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from live-cell imaging experiments.

claim: When MORs and DORs were activated simultaneously with [Met5]-enkephalin, desensitization of MORs was facilitated.
source: When MORs and DORs were activated simultaneously with [Met5]-enkephalin, desensitization of MORs was facilitated but internalization was not increased.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: When MORs and DORs were activated simultaneously with [Met5]-enkephalin, internalization was not increased.
source: When MORs and DORs were activated simultaneously with [Met5]-enkephalin, desensitization of MORs was facilitated but internalization was not increased.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from live-cell imaging experiments.

claim: MORs and DORs expressed in single striatal cholinergic interneurons function independently.
source: Together, these results indicate that while MORs and DORs are expressed in single striatal cholinergic interneurons, the two receptors function independently.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: Three opioid receptor-subtypes, µ (MOR), δ (DOR), and κ (KOR) are known to be distributed in many brain areas.
source: Three opioid receptor-subtypes, µ (MOR), δ (DOR), and κ (KOR) are known to be distributed in many brain areas (Le Merrer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation to prior literature.

claim: The co-expression of opioid receptor-subtypes in individual neurons could provide new pharmacological targets for analgesia while avoiding side effects associated with the activation of a single opioid receptor subtype.
source: The co-expression of opioid receptor-subtypes in individual neurons has steadily gained attention because possible cross-interactions between the receptors could provide new pharmacological targets for analgesia while avoiding the side effects associated with the activation of a single opioid receptor subtype (Fujita et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as a rationale for studying co-expression, with a citation to prior literature.

claim: There is evidence from biochemical and fluorescent imaging studies to support the existence of MOR-DOR heterodimers.
source: Although there is evidence from biochemical and fluorescent imaging studies to support the existence of MOR-DOR heterodimers (Cahill and Ong, 2018), those studies required the use of heterologous expression and genetically modified receptors to enable experimental detection.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior research with a citation.

claim: Studies supporting MOR-DOR heterodimers required the use of heterologous expression and genetically modified receptors.
source: Although there is evidence from biochemical and fluorescent imaging studies to support the existence of MOR-DOR heterodimers (Cahill and Ong, 2018), those studies required the use of heterologous expression and genetically modified receptors to enable experimental detection.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of prior research methods.

claim: Only a small population of dimers exist and interact in a time scale of milliseconds, resulting in a proposed 'kiss-and-run' model of receptor dimer interaction.
source: In addition, an increasing number of studies suggest that only a small population of dimers exist and interact in a time scale of milliseconds, resulting in a proposed 'kiss-and-run' model of receptor dimer interaction (Gurevich and Gurevich, 2008; Kasai and Kusumi, 2014; Calebiro and Sungaworn, 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior research with citations.

claim: There is no clear evidence that endogenously expressed MORs and DORs form stable heterodimers.
source: Thus, there is still no clear evidence that endogenously expressed MORs and DORs form stable heterodimers.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature that motivates the current study.

claim: Opioid receptors are generally expressed in low densities in neuronal tissues, thus detection of subcellular co-localization is often ambiguous.
source: The major challenge for testing these possible interactions in native tissue is the fact that opioid receptors are generally expressed in low densities in neuronal tissues, thus detection of subcellular co-localization is often ambiguous.
evidence: This is stated as a technical challenge in the field.

claim: Functional readout using electrophysiological measurement is a powerful tool to detect MOR-DOR co-expression in single neurons.
source: Functional readout using electrophysiological measurement is a powerful tool to detect MOR-DOR co-expression in single neurons but there are few such studies (Egan and North, 1981; Chieng et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated as a methodological advantage with citations to prior studies.

claim: The striatum plays an important role in motivation, sensorimotor function, goal-directed learning, and drug addiction.
source: The striatum is a subcortical structure in the forebrain that plays an important role in motivation, sensorimotor function, goal-directed learning, and drug addiction (Kreitzer, 2009; Castro and Bruchas, 2019).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.

claim: The largest portion of neurons in the striatum are medium spiny GABAergic projecting neurons that produce opioid peptides including enkephalin and dynorphin.
source: The largest portion of neurons are medium spiny GABAergic projecting neurons that are also known to produce opioid peptides including enkephalin (µ-and δ-agonists) and dynorphin (κ-agonists).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about striatal anatomy.

claim: All opioid receptor-subtypes have been located in the striatum by various techniques.
source: The striatum consists of a heterogeneous structure where all opioid receptor-subtypes have been located by various techniques (Le Merrer et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: MOR-binding sites are primarily detected in the striosomal patches.
source: MOR-binding sites are primarily detected in the striosomal patches, whereas DOR and KOR binding sites are found in both matrix and patches (Herkenham and Pert, 1981; Tempel and Zukin, 1987; Kitchen et al., 1997; Banghart et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior studies.

claim: DOR and KOR binding sites are found in both matrix and patches of the striatum.
source: MOR-binding sites are primarily detected in the striosomal patches, whereas DOR and KOR binding sites are found in both matrix and patches (Herkenham and Pert, 1981; Tempel and Zukin, 1987; Kitchen et al., 1997; Banghart et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior studies.

claim: Cholinergic interneurons comprise only 1–2% of all neurons in the striatum.
source: Cholinergic interneurons (ChIs) comprise only a small population (1–2% of all neurons) and are scattered throughout the striatum.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about striatal anatomy.

claim: Cholinergic interneurons are scattered throughout the striatum.
source: Cholinergic interneurons (ChIs) comprise only a small population (1–2% of all neurons) and are scattered throughout the striatum.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about striatal anatomy.

claim: Cholinergic interneurons function as an important regulator of the synaptic activity within the striatum including the local release of dopamine.
source: These neurons function as an important regulator of the synaptic activity within the striatum including the local release of dopamine (Cai et al., 2021; Yorgason et al., 2017; Threlfell et al., 2012; Cachope et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior studies.

claim: ChIs are spontaneously active neurons that release acetylcholine in brain slices and in vivo.
source: ChIs are spontaneously active neurons that release acetylcholine in brain slices and in vivo (Wilson et al., 1990; Bennett and Wilson, 1999; Zhou et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations to prior studies.

claim: The firing rate of ChIs is inhibited, and the membrane potential is hyperpolarized following the application of δ- but not µ-agonists.
source: The firing rate of these neurons is inhibited, and the membrane potential is hyperpolarized following the application of δ- but not µ-agonists (Jiang and North, 1992).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior research with a citation.

claim: Other studies report the presence of functional MORs in ChIs.
source: Other studies, however, report the presence of functional MORs in these neurons (Jabourian et al., 2005; Britt and McGehee, 2008; Ponterio et al., 2013; Mamaligas et al., 2016; Muñoz et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from prior research with citations.

claim: Various ChI subpopulations may contain segregated MORs and DORs.
source: It is possible that various ChI subpopulations contain segregated MORs and DORs (Jabourian et al., 2005; Britt and McGehee, 2008; Laurent et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a possibility based on prior research with citations.

claim: There is no evidence demonstrating that MORs and DORs are co-localized on ChIs.
source: To date, there is no evidence demonstrating that MORs and DORs are co-localized on ChIs.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature that motivates the current study.

claim: NAI-A594 is a labeling reagent that specifically binds opioid receptors and covalently tags them with the fluorophore Alexa-594.
source: Naltrexamine-acylimidazole-alexa594 (NAI-A594; Figure 1A–a) is a labeling reagent that has been shown to specifically bind opioid receptors and then covalently tag them with the fluorophore Alexa-594 to MORs in brain slices (Arttamangkul et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated as a property of the reagent with a citation to prior work.

claim: The labeling of NAI-A594 is based on traceless affinity labeling approach.
source: The labeling of this molecule is based on traceless affinity labeling approach (Hayashi and Hamachi, 2012; Shiraiwa et al., 2020), in which the naltrexamine moiety acts as a ligand that guides specific binding to opioid receptors.
evidence: This is stated as the mechanism of the labeling reagent with citations.

claim: The naltrexamine moiety acts as a ligand that guides specific binding to opioid receptors.
source: The labeling of this molecule is based on traceless affinity labeling approach (Hayashi and Hamachi, 2012; Shiraiwa et al., 2020), in which the naltrexamine moiety acts as a ligand that guides specific binding to opioid receptors.
evidence: This is stated as the mechanism of the labeling reagent.

claim: Once NAI-A594 is bound, the fluorophore is transferred to the receptor by the reaction of the acylimidazole group with an amino acid side chain nucleophile, and the guide ligand (naltrexamine) is cleaved and released from the binding pocket.
source: Once bound, the fluorophore is transferred to the receptor by the reaction of the acylimidazole group with an amino acid side chain nucleophile, and at the same time, the guide ligand (naltrexamine) is cleaved and released from the binding pocket (Figure 1A–b).
evidence: This is stated as the mechanism of the labeling reagent and illustrated in Figure 1A-b.

claim: Labeling of striatal slices from wild-type rats with NAI-A594 revealed striosomal patches.
source: The labeling of striatal slices from wild-type rats with NAI-A594 revealed striosomal patches, regions that are known to contain abundant MORs (Figure 1B–a and Arttamangkul et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1B-a.

claim: MOR-binding sites in the patches persisted when DORs were blocked with ICI-174,864.
source: The MOR-binding sites in the patches persisted when DORs were blocked with a selective antagonist ICI-174,864 (Figure 1B-b).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1B-b.

claim: Fluorescent labeling of the whole striatum was greatly diminished when the MOR selective antagonist, CTAP, was included in NAI-A594 solution.
source: In contrast, fluorescent labeling of the whole striatum was greatly diminished when the MOR selective antagonist, CTAP, was included in NAI-A594 solution (Figure 1B–c).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1B-c.

claim: Most of the labeling in the striatum were at MORs.
source: These results suggest that most of the labeling in the striatum were at MORs.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations with selective antagonists.

claim: Large neurons with a few dendrites near the boundary of the striosomal patches were fluorescently tagged with NAI-A594.
source: Large neurons with a few dendrites near the boundary of the striosomal patches were also fluorescently tagged (Figure 1B–d).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1B-d.

claim: The cell morphology and location of large neurons near the boundary of striosomal patches suggested that they were most likely ChI neurons.
source: The cell morphology and location of these neurons suggested that they were most likely ChI neurons (Brimblecombe and Cragg, 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on morphology and location with a citation to prior knowledge.

claim: The labeled receptors on large neurons near striosomal patches could be either MORs or DORs, due to the ability of NAI-A594 to label both receptors.
source: The labeled receptors on these large neurons, however, could be either MORs or DORs, due to the ability of NAI-A594 to label both receptors (Arttamangkul et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the properties of the labeling reagent.

claim: NAI-A488 at 30 and 100 nM reacted similarly with both FDOR and FMOR.
source: The results showed that NAI-A488 at 30 and 100 nM reacted similarly with both receptors (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1—source data 2, for red and green bands, respectively).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from western blot analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The labeling of FDOR and FMOR by NAI-A488 was specific, as it could be completely blocked by addition of the opioid antagonist naloxone.
source: The labeling of FDOR and FMOR by NAI-A488 was specific, as it could be completely blocked by addition of the opioid antagonist naloxone (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from western blot analysis shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Alexa488-labeled receptors are detected even after denaturing gel electrophoresis, confirming that the fluorophore is covalently bound to the receptors.
source: The fact that Alexa488-labeled receptors are detected even after denaturing gel electrophoresis confirms that the fluorophore is covalently bound to the receptors.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the western blot experimental results.

claim: The labeling curves for NAI-A488 reacted FDORs and FMORs were similar and saturated at about 100 nM.
source: The labeling curves for NAI-A488 reacted FDORs and FMORs were similar and saturated at about 100 nM.
evidence: This is an experimental observation from on-cell western assay.

claim: The labeling coefficients of NAI-A488 for FDOR and FMOR were comparable, with apparent Kd values of 7.1 ± 2.8 nM for FDOR and 3.3 ± 0.7 nM for FMOR.
source: The labeling coefficients were also comparable, with apparent Kd values of 7.1 ± 2.8 nM for FDOR and 3.3 ± 0.7 nM for FMOR (two-tailed, unpaired t-test, p = 0.2543, n = 3 experiments performed in triplicate).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from on-cell western assay with statistical analysis.

claim: The fluorescent NAI compound effectively and covalently labeled MORs and DORs.
source: Thus, the fluorescent NAI compound effectively and covalently labeled MORs and DORs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the biochemical experiments.

claim: Patch-like structures were present in the striatum of the ChAT-GFP mice following incubation with NAI-A594.
source: As previously observed, patch-like structures were present in the striatum of the ChAT-GFP mice following incubation with NAI-A594 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ChAT-GFP neurons were found scattered throughout the striatum.
source: The ChAT-GFP neurons were found scattered throughout the striatum (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The plasma membrane of GFP-positive perikarya, dendrites and axon terminals were Alexa 594 positive.
source: The plasma membrane of GFP-positive perikarya, dendrites and axon terminals were also Alexa 594 positive (Figure 2C&E for NAI-A594 staining and D&F for the merged images of NAI-A594 labeling and GFP).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2C-F.

claim: GFP-negative neurons, presumably medium spiny neurons, were also labeled with NAI-A594.
source: There are GFP-negative neurons, presumably medium spiny neurons that were also labeled with NAI-A594 (Figure 2C&D).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2C-D.

claim: All GFP-positive neurons reacted with NAI-A594 (n = 246 from seven male and six female mice).
source: Live-cell imaging experiments revealed all GFP-positive neurons reacted with NAI-A594 (n = 246 from seven male and six female mice).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from live-cell imaging.

claim: There was a partial decrease of the fluorescence on the plasma membrane of CTAP-treated neurons as compared to experiments with NAI-A594 alone.
source: The results show a partial decrease of the fluorescence on the plasma membrane of CTAP-treated neurons as compared to experiments with NAI-A594 alone (see Figure 3A–b and Figure 3A-a).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3A.

claim: In the presence of SDM25N, the fluorescence staining was further reduced as compared to CTAP-treated cells.
source: In the presence of SDM25N, the fluorescence staining was further reduced as compared to CTAP-treated cells (Figure 3A–c and Figure 3A-b).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The combination of SDM25N and CTAP completely blocked the labeling of ChAT-GFP neurons.
source: Finally, the combination of SDM25N and CTAP completely blocked the labeling of ChAT-GFP neurons (Figure 3A–d).
evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Average mean fluorescence intensity of NAI-A594-labeled cells in the dorsal striatum was ~20% higher than in ventral striatum.
source: Average mean fluorescence intensity of NAI-A594-labeled cells in the dorsal striatum was ~20 % higher than in ventral striatum (mean fluorescence± SD = 170.7 ± 57.6 for dorsal, n = 52 and 140.9 ± 47.6 for ventral n = 47; ordinary one-way ANOVA, Sidak's test, p = 0.0100 and n = numbers of GFP-positive neurons, Figure 3C, Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: When DOR was measured by co-incubating with NAI-A594 plus CTAP, the fluorescent intensity on neurons in the dorsal striatum was reduced to 68% of that observed with NAI-A594 alone.
source: When DOR was measured by co-incubating with NAI-A594 plus CTAP, the fluorescent intensity on neurons in the dorsal striatum was reduced to 68% of that observed with NAI-A594 alone (mean fluorescence± SD = 115.5 ± 49.7, n = 41 as compared to the mean fluorescence of NAI-A594 = 170.7 ± 57.6 for dorsal, n = 52; p < 0.0001, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The fluorescence of neurons in the ventral striatum was reduced to 61% of NAI-A594 alone when DOR was measured by co-incubating with NAI-A594 plus CTAP.
source: Similarly, the fluorescence of neurons in the ventral striatum was reduced to 61% of NAI-A594 alone (mean fluorescence± SD = 85.8 ± 47.3, n = 35 as compared to the mean fluorescence of NAI-A594 = 140.9 ± 47.6 for ventral, n = 47; p < 0.0001, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Fluorescence of Alexa594-labeled ChAT-GFP neurons in the presence of CTAP was similar to the labeling of the cholinergic neurons from MOR knockout mice.
source: Fluorescence of Alexa594-labeled ChAT-GFP neurons in the presence of CTAP was found to be similar to the labeling of the cholinergic neurons from MOR knockout mice (Figure 3—source data 1: Figure 3—figure supplement 1—source data 2), suggesting that the blockade of NAI-A594 labeling at MORs by CTAP was sufficient.
evidence: This is an experimental observation with comparison to MOR knockout mice.

claim: When the detection of MOR was determined by NAI-A594 in the presence of SDM25N, the fluorescent intensity of labeled cells was only ~37% and ~47% of that observed with NAI-A594 alone in the dorsal and ventral striatum, respectively.
source: Interestingly, when the detection of MOR was determined by NAI-A594 in the presence of SDM25N, the fluorescent intensity of labeled cells was only ~37% and ~ 47% of that observed with NAI-A594 alone in the dorsal and ventral striatum, respectively (mean fluorescence± SD = 63.9 ± 19.5, n = 48 as compared to the mean fluorescence of NAI-A594 = 170.7 ± 57.6, n = 52 for dorsal, and 65.7 ± 25.5, n = 22 as compared to the mean fluorescence of NAI-A594 = 140.9 ± 47.6, n = 47 for ventral; p < 0.0001 for both, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: There was a large difference between fluorescent staining of DOR and MOR in dorsal part of the striatum.
source: There was a large difference between fluorescent staining of DOR and MOR in dorsal part of the striatum (115.5 ± 49.7, n = 41 for DOR vs. 63.9 ± 19.5, n = 48 for MOR, one-way ANOVA, p < 0.0001), while the relative fluorescence of DOR and MOR in the ventral striatum was comparable (85.8 ± 47.3, n = 35 for DOR vs. 65.7 ± 25.5, n = 22 for MOR, p = 0.612, Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an experimental observation with statistical analysis shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Cholinergic interneurons contain both MORs and DORs.
source: Thus, these results indicate that: (i) cholinergic interneurons contain both MORs and DORs and (ii) expression of DORs appears to be higher than MORs in the dorsal striatum but not different from MORs in the ventral striatum.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fluorescence labeling experiments.

claim: Expression of DORs appears to be higher than MORs in the dorsal striatum but not different from MORs in the ventral striatum.
source: Thus, these results indicate that: (i) cholinergic interneurons contain both MORs and DORs and (ii) expression of DORs appears to be higher than MORs in the dorsal striatum but not different from MORs in the ventral striatum.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the fluorescence labeling experiments.

claim: Cholinergic interneurons are spontaneously active in mouse brain slice preparations with a firing rate of 1–2 Hz.
source: Cholinergic interneurons are spontaneously active in mouse brain slice preparations with a firing rate of 1–2 Hz (Ponterio et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a citation.

claim: The average spontaneous firing rate of the GFP-positive neurons was 1.5 ± 0.1 Hz (n = 9 cells from three male and three female mice).
source: The average spontaneous firing rate of the GFP-positive neurons was 1.5 ± 0.1 Hz (n = 9 cells from three male and three female mice).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings.

claim: DAMGO (1 µM) completely inhibited firing of ChIs, and this inhibition was reversed following application of CTAP (1 µM).
source: The µ-agonist, DAMGO (1 µM) completely inhibited firing, and this inhibition was reversed following application of CTAP (1 µM).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: Deltorphin (1 µM) stopped firing of ChIs and this was reversed by SDM25N (0.5 µM).
source: Subsequent application of the δ-agonist, deltorphin (1 µM) also stopped firing and this was reversed by SDM25N (0.5 µM, Figure 4A).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings shown in Figure 4.

claim: ChIs co-express functional MORs and DORs.
source: The results indicate that ChIs co-express functional MORs and DORs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological experiments.

claim: The firing frequency of ChIs from wild-type mice was similar to that of ChAT-GFP (1.4 ± 0.1 Hz, n = 67 cells from fourteen male and eleven female mice).
source: The firing frequency of ChIs from wild-type mice was similar to that of ChAT-GFP (1.4 ± 0.1 Hz, n = 67 cells from fourteen male and eleven female mice, compared to the firing rate of ChAT-GFP neurons of 1.5 ± 0.1 Hz, n = 9 cells, two-tailed, unpaired t-test, p = 0.6490).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings with statistical analysis.

claim: DAMGO (1 µM) caused an inhibition of firing activity by 98.0% ± 1.2% (n = 7).
source: DAMGO (1 µM) caused an inhibition of firing activity by 98.0% ± 1.2% (n = 7) and increasing the concentration to (10 µM) had no further effect (Table 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings shown in Table 1.

claim: Deltorphin (1 µM) caused a total inhibition of firing (96.6% ± 2.7% n = 10).
source: Deltorphin (1 µM) also caused a total inhibition of firing (96.6% ± 2.7% n = 10).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings shown in Table 1.

claim: ME (10 µM) resulted in a complete inhibition of the spontaneous firing (99.4% ± 0.6%, n = 11).
source: Application of a saturating concentration of [Met5]-enkephalin (ME, 10 µM) resulted in a complete inhibition of the spontaneous firing (99.4% ± 0.6%, n = 11) and ME (1 µM) reduced the firing by 92.6% ± 2.6% of baseline (n = 12).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings shown in Table 1.

claim: ME (1 µM) reduced the firing by 92.6% ± 2.6% of baseline (n = 12).
source: Application of a saturating concentration of [Met5]-enkephalin (ME, 10 µM) resulted in a complete inhibition of the spontaneous firing (99.4% ± 0.6%, n = 11) and ME (1 µM) reduced the firing by 92.6% ± 2.6% of baseline (n = 12).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings shown in Table 1.

claim: When CTAP was used to block activity of MORs, ME (1 µM) inhibited the firing activity by 97.7% ± 1.4% (n = 6).
source: When CTAP was used to block activity of MORs, ME (1 µM) inhibited the firing activity by 97.7% ± 1.4% (n = 6) (Table 1, Table 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings shown in Table 1.

claim: When DORs were blocked with SDM25N, ME (1 µM) reduced the firing rate by 97.3% ± 1.7% (n = 6).
source: When DORs were blocked with SDM25N, ME (1 µM) reduced the firing rate by 97.3% ± 1.7% (n = 6, Table 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings shown in Table 1.

claim: ME acted on both MORs and DORs.
source: Thus, as expected, ME acted on both receptors.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the electrophysiological experiments with selective antagonists.

claim: Morphine (10 µM) only partially decreased the firing by 79.4% ± 5.0% (n = 10).
source: Morphine (10 µM) only partially decreased the firing by 79.4% ± 5.0% (n = 10) and morphine (1 µM) reduced the firing rate by 48.9% ± 8.3% (n = 8) (Table 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings shown in Table 1.

claim: Morphine (1 µM) reduced the firing rate by 48.9% ± 8.3% (n = 8).
source: Morphine (10 µM) only partially decreased the firing by 79.4% ± 5.0% (n = 10) and morphine (1 µM) reduced the firing rate by 48.9% ± 8.3% (n = 8) (Table 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings shown in Table 1.

claim: CTAP blocked the inhibition induced by morphine (10.0% ± 3.7% inhibition in 10 µM morphine +1 µM CTAP, n = 7).
source: In addition, CTAP blocked the inhibition induced by morphine (10.0% ± 3.7% inhibition in 10 µM morphine +1 µM CTAP, n = 7) (Table 1).
evidence: This is an experimental observation from electrophysiological recordings shown in Table 1.

claim: The application of saturating concentrations of efficacious agonist commonly results in the desensitization of MORs and DORs in many brain areas.
source: The application of saturating concentrations of efficacious agonist commonly results in the desensitization of MORs and DORs in many brain areas (Williams et al., 2013; Gendron et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with citations.
